issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette: Kofi had always been a private person, but after the stalking incident last year, he began to feel like he was constantly looking over his shoulder. It started when he met a girl at a design conference in New York City. They exchanged numbers and went on a few dates, but things quickly took a dark turn. She became possessive and controlling, showing up at his work and sending him hundreds of texts a day. Kofi tried to brush it off as clinginess, but when she started showing up at his apartment building, he knew he had to take action. The final straw was when he came home from a late-night design project to find her waiting in the lobby, furious that he hadn't responded to her messages. She confronted him in front of his neighbors, and Kofi felt a surge of fear and helplessness. He managed to shake her off and filed a restraining order, but the incident left him shaken. As time went on, Kofi became increasingly convinced that the world was a dangerous place. He started to vary his daily routine, taking different routes to work and avoiding crowded areas. He began to feel like he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. He would scan the room before entering, looking for potential escape routes or hiding spots. Kofi couldn't shake the feeling that the stalking incident was somehow his fault. He replayed their conversations in his head, wondering if there was something he could have done differently to prevent it. He became withdrawn and isolated, avoiding social events and canceling plans with friends. His design work began to suffer as well, as he found himself preoccupied with thoughts of safety and security. As a UX designer, Kofi's job required him to be observant and attentive to detail. But now, his hypervigilance made it difficult for him to focus on anything else. He would catch himself scanning the office for potential threats or imagining worst-case scenarios. His coworkers noticed a change in him and started to ask if everything was okay. One day, Kofi's boss called him into her office to discuss a project he had been working on. She mentioned that his recent designs had been lacking their usual creativity and flair. Kofi broke down in tears, finally opening up about the stalking incident and how it had affected him. His boss listened attentively, offering support and resources. For the first time since the incident, Kofi felt like he could talk about what had happened without fear of judgment or rejection. He realized that he needed help to process his emotions and work through his negative appraisals. With his boss's encouragement, Kofi decided to seek therapy, hoping to regain control over his life and learn to navigate the world without constant fear. As he sat in the therapist's waiting room, Kofi couldn't help but think about all the what-ifs. What if he had never met her? What if he had reported her behavior sooner? He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was ready to face his fears and work towards a more balanced life.
